system_overview: This specification models the abstract consensus problem, in which a set of processes must cooperatively choose a single value from a set of proposed values. It captures the most fundamental safety requirement of consensus: that at most one value is ever chosen. The specification abstracts away individual processes entirely and focuses only on the set of chosen values.
actors_and_components: There are no explicit process identities or roles in this specification. The system is modeled purely in terms of the set of values that can be proposed and the set of values that have been chosen. The set of proposable values is a declared constant.
state_variables: The system tracks a single piece of state: the set of values that have been chosen so far.
initial_state: Initially, no value has been chosen. The set of chosen values is empty.
actions: There is exactly one kind of transition: if no value has been chosen yet, the system may select any single value from the set of proposable values and record it as the chosen value. Once a value is chosen, no further transitions are enabled -- the system reaches a terminal state.
safety_properties: The chosen set is always a subset of the declared value set, and the number of chosen values never exceeds one. In other words, at most one value is ever chosen, and once chosen it cannot be revoked or changed. This is expressed as an invariant that the cardinality of the chosen set is at most one and all elements are valid values.
liveness_properties: Under a weak fairness assumption on the choosing action, a value is eventually chosen. Without that fairness assumption, the base specification permits the system to stutter forever without choosing any value.
model_bounds: The set of proposable values is a finite constant. For model checking, it is typically instantiated with a small set (for example, three model values).
additional_assumptions: The specification includes a machine-checked proof that the safety invariant (at most one value chosen) holds. The proof uses standard finite-set cardinality reasoning. The specification also extends standard arithmetic and finite-set library modules, and uses a proof-system backend for formal verification.
